---
title: "From linguistic records to probabilities"
---

A statistical analysis does not begin when we fit a model. It begins when we decide what one observation is.

An audio file might become a table with one row per speaker, one row per word, one row per vowel token, or several rows per vowel token. A corpus might become a table of documents, sentences, tokens, or lexical types. Each choice preserves some distinctions and removes others. A later model can only describe the distinctions that the dataset retains.

This module develops that point in two stages. The first stage concerns linguistic records and numerical patterns. The second builds a probability model one object at a time.

## From records to comparisons

We begin with [turning linguistic records into data](linguistic-data.qmd). That page separates a stored record from the unit represented by one row. It also asks which identifiers repeat and which variation disappears during aggregation.

The next page turns [a research question into a comparison](making-sense-of-data.qmd). It specifies the response, the linguistic predictor, the observations being compared, and the estimand. These decisions state what a later numerical result is supposed to mean.

[Zipf's law](zipfs-law.qmd) supplies the first worked linguistic pattern. The rank and frequency calculation is simple enough to do by hand, but its interpretation is not. The example separates describing a curve from explaining why that curve appears.

## From possibilities to a probability model

The probability sequence has a strict order.

1. A [sample space](possibilities-and-events.qmd) lists the possible outcomes under a declared representation.
2. An [event](events.qmd) groups outcomes that answer a linguistic question in the same way.
3. A [sigma-algebra](event-spaces.qmd) states which of those groups the model can measure.
4. A [generated sigma-algebra](generating-event-spaces.qmd) is the smallest sigma-algebra forced by a chosen set of distinctions.
5. A [probability measure](probability-measures.qmd) assigns coherent numerical mass to the measurable events.
6. [Mutual exclusivity](probability-concepts.qmd) states when two events cannot occur together.
7. [Joint probability](joint-probability-of-events.qmd) measures the event in which two properties occur together.
8. [Conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd) rescales probability within a stated event.
9. [The product rule](probability-factorization.qmd) reconstructs a joint probability from a conditional probability and its condition.
10. [Bayes' rule](bayes-rule.qmd) reverses the direction of a conditional probability while retaining event prevalence.
11. [Independence](independence.qmd) states when conditioning on one event does not change the probability of another.

Each page uses only objects introduced earlier in this list. The sequence stops after independence so that later numerical objects can be introduced in their own module.

## A question to carry through the module

For any linguistic dataset, keep asking the same question:

> Which represented outcomes and distinctions make this probability statement meaningful?

If the answer is not available, the numerical calculation may still be correct while the linguistic interpretation remains unsupported. The purpose of the foundations sequence is to make that representation visible before adding more elaborate models.

The [chapter dependency graph](../learning-path.qmd) places this chapter within the full course. Begin with [turning linguistic records into data](linguistic-data.qmd).
